First, the islands and cayes (such as Ranguana and Sapodilla) were not explicitly included in the main Anglo-Spanish treaties of the 18th century, nor in the 1859 Wyke-Aycinena Treaty between Guatemala and Britain. Construction began in the 1930s and was largely completed by the 1950s, with the final sections finished by the 1960s. Fifth, the Belizean–Guatemalan territorial dispute is deeply rooted in the legacy of British colonialism, and both countries can be seen as victims of historical circumstances shaped by imperial powers and should both be adequately compensated by the British. Finally, it is a fact that some Maya communities in Belize have familial, linguistic, and cultural ties to Maya in Guatemala and are therefore also victims of the British abuses. _N_08zn95FY.text: Although Turkey argues that Greece forfeited sovereignty over the Aegean and Dodecanese islands by militarizing them, the treaties themselves do not support this interpretation. The Treaty of Lausanne (1923) explicitly confirmed Greek sovereignty over islands such as Lesbos, Chios, Samos, and Ikaria, while imposing certain restrictions on fortifications. Yet nowhere does the treaty stipulate that sovereignty would revert to Turkey if those conditions were violated. International law recognizes sovereignty transfers as permanent unless a treaty expressly provides for reversion, which is not the case here. The Treaty of Paris (1947) likewise transferred the Dodecanese from Italy to Greece with a demilitarization clause, but Turkey was not a signatory to that treaty and thus lacks standing to enforce its provisions. Furthermore, the principle of self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter supersedes demilitarization obligations if a state faces imminent threat. Following Turkey’s 1974 invasion of Cyprus and the creation of the Aegean Army with amphibious capabilities directly across from the Greek islands, Athens reasonably judged militarization a matter of survival. Even the International Court of Justice has emphasized that sovereignty cannot be undone retroactively due to alleged breaches of ancillary obligations. Historically, Greece’s sovereignty was not a “gift” from Turkey but the outcome of international settlements following the Balkan Wars and World War I, when the Great Powers decided that these predominantly Greek-populated islands should belong to Greece. Turkey’s narrative reframes internationally recognized treaties as conditional bargains, but the legal record shows otherwise: Greece’s sovereignty is settled law, and disputes about militarization fall under security concerns, not territorial ownership.
